contenido: 2. We have already spoken on other occasions, especially in the encyclical Immortale Dei, about the so-called modern freedoms, separating what is good in them from what is bad in them. We have demonstrated at the same time that everything good that these freedoms present is as old as the truth itself, and that the Church has always approved it with good will and has always incorporated it into the daily practice of its life. The novelty added modernly, if we must tell the truth, is nothing more than an authentic corruption produced by the turbulence of the time and by the immoderate fever of revolutions. But since there are many who persist in seeing, even in the vicious aspects of these liberties, the supreme glory of our times and the necessary foundation of every political constitution, as if it were impossible to conceive the perfect government of the State without these liberties, it has seemed necessary to us, for the usefulness of all, to treat this matter with particular attention.

3. The direct object of this exposition is moral freedom, considered both in the individual and in society. It is appropriate, however, at the beginning to briefly present some ideas about natural freedom, because although this is totally different from moral freedom, it is, nevertheless, the source and principle from which all species of freedom are born and spontaneously derived. The right judgment and common sense of all men, the sure voice of Nature, recognizes this freedom only in beings that have intelligence or reason; and it is this freedom that makes man responsible for all his actions. It couldn't be any other way. Because while animals obey only their senses and under the exclusive impulse of nature they seek what is useful to them and flee what is harmful to them, man has reason as his guide in each and every one of the actions of his life. But reason, in view of the goods of this world, judges of each and every one of them that they can either exist or not exist; and concluding, for this reason, that none of the aforementioned goods is absolutely necessary, reason gives the will the power to choose what it wants. Now, man can judge the contingency of these goods that we have mentioned, because he has a soul of a simple, spiritual nature, capable of thinking; a soul that, by its own entity, does not come from corporeal things nor does it depend on them for its preservation, but, created immediately by God and far superior to the common condition of bodies, it has its own way of life and a no less proper way of acting; This is what explains why man, with the intellectual knowledge of the immutable and necessary essences of good and truth, discovers with certainty that these particular goods are in no way necessary goods. In this way, affirming that the human soul is free of all mortal elements and endowed with the faculty of thinking is equivalent to establishing natural freedom on its most solid foundation.

4. Now: just as the Catholic Church has been the highest propagator and most constant defender of the simplicity, spirituality and immortality of the human soul, so is the Church the strongest defender of freedom. The Church has always taught these two realities and defends them as dogmas of faith. And not only this. Faced with the attacks of heretics and promoters of novelties, it has been the Church that took charge of the defense of freedom and that freed this most excellent quality of man from ruin. The history of theology demonstrates the energetic reaction of the Church against the crazy attempts of the Manichaeans and other heretics. And, in more recent times, everyone knows the vigorous effort that the Church made, first at the Council of Trent and then against the disciples of Jansenius, to defend the freedom of man, without allowing fatalism to take root in any time or place.

5. Freedom is, therefore, as we have said, the exclusive heritage of beings endowed with intelligence or reason. Considered in its very nature, this freedom is nothing other than the power to choose between the means that are suitable to achieve a given end, in the sense that he who has the power to choose one thing among many is the master of his own actions. Now, since everything that one chooses as a means to obtain something else belongs to the genus of the so-called useful good, and the good by its very nature has the power to move the will, from this it is concluded that freedom is characteristic of the will, or more precisely, it is the will itself, insofar as it, when acting, has the power to choose. But the movement of the will is impossible if intellectual knowledge does not precede it, illuminating it like a torch, that is, the good desired by the will is necessarily good as previously known by reason. All the more so since in all human volitions the choice is subsequent to the judgment on the truth of the proposed goods and on the order of preference that must be observed in them. But judgment is, without a doubt, an act of reason, not of the will. If freedom, therefore, resides in the will, which is by its very nature an appetite obedient to reason, it follows that freedom, like the will, has as its object a good in accordance with reason. However, since reason and will are imperfect faculties, it can happen, and often happens, that reason proposes to the will an object that, being in reality evil, presents a deceptive appearance of good, and that the will applies itself to it. But just as the possibility of error and error in fact is a defect that indicates an imperfect understanding, so also adhering to a deceptive and feigned good, even though it is an indication of free will, just as illness is a sign of life, nevertheless constitutes a defect of freedom. In a similar way, the will, by the sole fact of its dependence on reason, when it desires an object that deviates from right reason, incurs the radical defect of corrupting and abusing freedom. And this is the reason why God, infinitely perfect, and who, because he is extremely intelligent and essentially good, is extremely free, cannot in any way will moral evil; nor can the blessed in heaven want it, because of the contemplation of the supreme good. This was the objection that Saint Augustine and other authors wisely raised against the Pelagians. If the possibility of departing from good belonged to the essence and perfection of freedom, then God, Jesus Christ, the angels and the blessed, all of whom lack this power, would either not be free or, at least, would not be free with the same perfection as man in a state of trial and imperfection.

6. This being the condition of human freedom, freedom needed protection and help capable of directing all its movements towards good and separating them from evil. Otherwise, freedom would have been seriously detrimental to man. First of all, a law was necessary, that is, a rule of what to do and what to avoid. Law, in the proper sense, cannot occur in animals, which act out of necessity, since they carry out all their acts by natural instinct and cannot adopt any other way of action for themselves. On the other hand, beings who enjoy freedom have the power to act or not act, to act in this or that way, because the choice of the object of their volition is subsequent to the judgment of reason, to which we have referred before. This judgment establishes not only what is good or bad by nature, but also what is good and therefore should be done, and what is bad and therefore should be avoided. That is, reason prescribes to the will what it should seek and what it should avoid so that man can one day achieve his ultimate goal, to which he must direct all his actions. And precisely this ordering of reason is what is called law. Therefore, the justification of the need for law for man must be sought first and radically in freedom itself, that is, in the need for the human will not to deviate from right reason. There is no statement more absurd and dangerous than this: that man, because he is naturally free, must live detached from all law. Because if this premise were true, the logical conclusion would be that it is essential to freedom to disagree with reason, while the true statement is the contradictory one, that is, that man, precisely because he is free, must live subject to the law. In this way it is the law that guides man in his action and it is the law that moves man, with the incentive of the reward and the fear of punishment, to do good and avoid evil. Such is the main of all laws, the natural law, written and engraved in the heart of each man, because it is the same human reason that commands man to do good and prohibits man from doing evil.

7. What has been said about the freedom of each individual is easily applicable to men united in civil society. Because what reason and natural law do in each man, human law, promulgated for the common good of citizens, does in those associated with it. Among these human laws there are some whose object consists of what is good or bad by nature, adding to the precept of practicing good and avoiding evil the appropriate sanction. The origin of these laws is in no way the State; because just as society is not the origin of human nature, in the same way society is not the source of the concordance of good and the discordance of evil with nature. Quite the opposite. These laws are prior to society itself, and their origin must be sought in natural law and, therefore, in eternal law. Therefore, the precepts of natural law included in human laws do not simply have the value of a positive law, but in addition, and mainly, they include a much higher and august power that comes from the natural law itself and from the eternal law. In this type of laws, the mission of the civil legislator is limited to achieving, through a common discipline, the obedience of citizens, punishing the perverse and vicious, to separate them from evil and return them to good, or to prevent, at least, that they harm society and harm their fellow citizens.

8. Therefore, the nature of human freedom, regardless of the field in which we consider it, in individuals or in the community, in the rulers or in the governed, includes the need to obey a supreme and eternal reason, which is none other than the authority of God imposing his commandments and prohibitions. And this most just dominion of God over men is so far from even suppressing or weakening human freedom, that what it does is precisely the opposite: defend and perfect it; because the true perfection of every created being consists in tending to its own end and achieving it. Now: the supreme end to which human freedom must aspire is none other than God himself.

9. The Church, taught by the teachings and examples of its divine Founder, has defended and propagated everywhere these precepts of profound and true doctrine, known even by the light of reason alone. The Church has never ceased to measure its mission with them and to educate Christian peoples in them. In regard to morals, the evangelical law not only far surpasses all pagan wisdom, but also openly calls man and enables him to a holiness unknown in ancient times, and, bringing him closer to God, puts him in possession of a more perfect freedom. In this way, the wonderful effectiveness of the Church in the defense and maintenance of the civil and political freedom of the people has always shone.

10. It is, furthermore, a very serious obligation to respect authority and obey just laws, thus leaving citizens defended from the injustice of criminals thanks to the vigilant effectiveness of the law. Legitimate power comes from God, and he who resists authority resists God's disposition. In this way, obedience is dignified in an extraordinary way, since obedience is paid to the most just and highest authority. But when there is no right to command, or something is commanded contrary to reason, to the eternal law, to the authority of God, it is right then to disobey men to obey God. Once the door to tyranny is thus closed, the entire State will not absorb it. The rights of each citizen, the rights of the family, the rights of all members of the State will be safe, and everyone will have ample participation in true freedom, which consists, as we have shown, in being able to live each one according to the laws and according to right reason.

11. If those who talk about freedom at every step understood by it the good and legitimate freedom that we have just described, no one would dare accuse the Church, with the unjust reproach they make of it, of being the enemy of the freedom of individuals and the freedom of the State. But there are already many who, imitating Lucifer, of whom is that criminal expression: I will not serve, understand by freedom what is a pure and absurd license. Such are the supporters of that widespread and powerful system, and who, taking the name of freedom itself, call themselves liberals.

12. Naturalism or rationalism in philosophy coincides with liberalism in morality and politics, since the followers of liberalism apply to morality and the practice of life the same principles established by the defenders of naturalism. Now: the fundamental principle of all rationalism is the sovereignty of human reason, which, denying the obedience due to divine and eternal reason and declaring itself independent, becomes the supreme principle, exclusive source and sole judge of truth. This is the claim of the aforementioned followers of liberalism; According to them there is no divine authority in practical life that must be obeyed; Each citizen is his own law. From here arises that so-called independent morality, which, separating the will, under the pretext of freedom, from the observance of divine commandments, grants man unlimited license. The ultimate consequences of these statements, especially in the social order, are easy to see. Because, when man is convinced that he has no superior over him, the immediate conclusion is to place the efficient cause of the civil and political community not in a principle exterior or superior to man, but in the free will of each one; derive political power from the multitude as a primary source. And just as individual reason is for the individual in his private life the only normative norm of his conduct, in the same way collective reason must be for everyone the only normative rule in the sphere of public life. Hence the number as a decisive force and the majority as the exclusive creator of right and duty.

13. It is true that not all defenders of liberalism agree with these opinions, terrible for their very monstrosity, openly contrary to the truth and cause, as we have seen, of the greatest evils. Compelled by the force of truth, many liberals recognize without shame and even spontaneously affirm that freedom, when it is exercised without considering any excess and with contempt for truth and justice, is a perverted freedom that degenerates into open license; and that, therefore, freedom must be directed and governed by right reason, and consequently must be subject to natural law and the eternal law of God. They think that this is enough and deny that the free man must submit to the laws that God wants to impose on him by a path other than that of natural reason. But by placing this limitation they are not consistent with themselves. Because if, as they admit and no one can reasonably deny, we must obey the will of God the legislator, because of man's total dependence on God and because of man's tendency towards God, the consequence is that no one can put limits or conditions on this legislative power of God without at the same time breaking the obedience due to God. Furthermore, if man's reason were to arrogate to itself the power to establish for itself the nature and extent of God's rights and its own obligations, respect for divine laws would be an appearance, not a reality, and man's judgment would be worth more than the authority and providence of God himself. It is necessary, therefore, that the standard of our life be continually and religiously adjusted not only to the eternal law, but also to each and every one of the other laws that God, in his infinite wisdom, in his infinite power and by whatever means he has seen fit, has communicated to us; laws that we can know with certainty through clear and indubitable signs. A need accentuated by the fact that this type of laws, having the same principle and the same author as the eternal law, agree entirely with reason, perfect natural law and also include the teaching of God himself, who, so that our understanding and our will do not fall into error, governs both benignly with his loving direction. Let what cannot and should not be separated be kept holy and inviolably united, and let God be served in all things, as natural reason itself commands, with all submission and obedience.

14. There are other liberals that are somewhat more moderate, but that does not make them more consistent with themselves; These liberals affirm that, indeed, divine laws should regulate the life and conduct of individuals, but not the life and conduct of the State; It is legal in political life to depart from the precepts of God and legislate without taking them into account at all. From this noble statement springs the pernicious consequence that the separation between Church and State is necessary. It is easy to understand the absurd error of these statements.

15. To give greater clarity to the points discussed, it is convenient to separately examine the various types of freedom, which some propose as achievements of our time. First of all, let us examine, in relation to individuals, that freedom so contrary to the virtue of religion, the so-called freedom of religion, a freedom founded on the thesis that each person can, at his discretion, profess the religion he prefers or not profess any. This thesis is contrary to the truth. Because of all the obligations of man, the greatest and most sacred is, without a doubt, that which commands us to give God the worship of religion and piety. This duty is the necessary consequence of our perpetual dependence on God, of our government by God, and of our first origin and supreme end, which is God. It must also be added that without the virtue of religion no authentic virtue is possible, because moral virtue is that virtue whose acts have as their object everything that leads us to God, considered the supreme and ultimate good of man; and for this reason, religion, whose office is to carry out everything that has as its direct and immediate end the honor of God, is the queen and the rule at the same time of all the virtues. And if you ask what religion to follow among so many religions that are opposed to each other, the answer is given in unison by reason and nature: the religion that God has commanded, and that is easily recognizable through certain external notes with which divine Providence has wanted to distinguish it, to avoid an error, which, in a matter of such importance, would imply disastrous consequences. For this reason, granting man this freedom of worship that we are talking about is equivalent to granting him the right to denature with impunity a most sacred obligation and to be unfaithful to it, abandoning good to surrender to evil. This, we have already said, is not freedom, it is a depravity of freedom and a slavery of the soul given over to sin.

16. Considered from the social and political point of view, this freedom of worship seeks that the State does not render any worship to God or does not authorize any public worship, that no worship is preferred to another, that everyone enjoys the same rights and that the people do not mean anything when they profess the Catholic religion. For these claims to be correct, it would be necessary that the State's duties towards God were null or could at least be violated with impunity by the State. Both assumptions are false. Because no one can doubt that the existence of civil society is the work of the will of God, whether this society is considered in its members, or in its form, which is the authority; now in its cause, now in the copious benefits it provides to man. It is God who has made man sociable and who has placed him among his fellow men, so that the natural demands that he cannot satisfy on his own can be satisfied within society. This is why it is necessary that the State, by the mere fact of being a society, recognizes God as Father and author and reveres and adores his power and dominion. Justice and reason prohibit, therefore, the atheism of the State, or, what would be equivalent to atheism, the indifferentism of the State in religious matters, and the indiscriminate legal equality of all religions. Since the public profession of a religion is therefore necessary in the State, the State must profess the only true religion, which is easily recognizable, especially in Catholic peoples, since the distinctive characters of the truth appear as if engraved in it. This is the religion that rulers must preserve and protect, if they want to serve the political community with prudent utility, as is their obligation. Because political power has been constituted for the benefit of the governed. And although the immediate goal of its action is to provide citizens with the prosperity of this earthly life, however, it should not diminish, but rather increase, the citizen's facilities to achieve the supreme and final good, in which lies the everlasting blessedness of man, and which he cannot reach if religion is neglected.

17. We have already spoken extensively about this point on other occasions. Now we just want to give a warning: freedom of religion is very harmful to true freedom, both for the rulers and the governed. Religion, on the other hand, is extremely beneficial for this freedom, because it places in God the first origin of power and imposes with maximum authority on rulers the obligation not to forget their duties, not to command with injustice or harshness and to govern the people with kindness and with an almost paternal love. On the other hand, religion commands citizens to submit to the legitimate powers as representatives of God and unites them to the rulers not only through obedience, but also with loving respect, prohibiting any revolution and any attempt that could disturb public order and tranquility, and which ultimately cause the freedom of citizens to be subjected to greater limitations. We leave aside the influence of religion on healthy morality and the influence of this morality on freedom itself. Reason demonstrates and history confirms this fact: the freedom, prosperity and greatness of a State are directly related to the morality of its men.

18. Let us now say a few words about freedom of speech and freedom of the press. It is almost unnecessary to affirm that the right to this freedom does not exist when it is exercised without any moderation, crossing all restraints and all limits. Because the right is a moral faculty that, as we have already said and it is worth repeating insistently, we cannot assume that it is granted by nature in the same way to truth and error, to virtue and vice. There is the right to propagate in society, with freedom and prudence, everything true and everything virtuous so that the greatest possible number of citizens can participate in the advantages of truth and good. But false opinions, the greatest mortal ailment of human understanding, and corrupting vices of the spirit and public morality must be repressed by public power to prevent their gradual spread, extremely harmful to society itself. The errors of depraved intellectuals exercise a true tyranny over the masses and must be repressed by law with the same energy as any other crime inflicted with violence on the weak. This repression is even more necessary, because the vast majority of citizens cannot in any way, or at most with great difficulty, protect themselves against the artifices of style and the subtleties of dialectic, especially when these and those are used to flatter the passions. If everyone is granted unlimited license in speaking and writing, nothing will remain sacred and inviolable. Not even those first truths will be excepted, those natural principles that constitute the noblest common heritage of all humanity. Thus, little by little, the truth is obscured by darkness and, as often happens, a numerous plague of pernicious errors takes over the field. Everything that license gains, freedom loses. The greatness and security of freedom are directly related to the brakes that oppose license. But in matters of opinion, left by God to the free discussion of men, each person is permitted to have the opinion that pleases him and to freely express his own opinion. Nature is not opposed to this, because this freedom never leads man to oppress the truth. On the contrary, it often leads to the discovery and manifestation of the truth.

19. Regarding the so-called freedom of teaching, the judgment that must be given is very similar. Only truth must penetrate the understanding, because in truth rational natures find their good, their end and their perfection; For this reason, the doctrine given to both the ignorant and the wise must have truth as its exclusive object, to direct the former towards the knowledge of the truth and to preserve the latter in possession of the truth. This is the foundation of the main obligation of those who teach: to extirpate error from understandings and effectively block the path to false theories. It is evident, therefore, that the freedom we are talking about, by attempting to arrogate to itself the right to teach everything at its whim, is in flagrant contradiction with reason and tends by its very nature to the most complete perversion of spirits. The public power cannot grant society this freedom of education without violating its own duties. A prohibition whose rigor increases for two reasons: because the authority of the teacher is very great in the eyes of the listeners and because there are very few disciples who can judge for themselves whether what the teacher explains to them is true or false.

20. Therefore it is necessary that this freedom, if it is to be virtuous, be circumscribed within certain limits, to prevent teaching from being converted with impunity into an instrument of corruption. Now: the truth, which must be the sole object of teaching, is of two kinds: one, natural; another, supernatural.

21. Much is also said about the so-called freedom of conscience. If this freedom is understood in the sense that it is lawful for each person, as he pleases, to worship God or not, it is sufficiently refuted by the arguments presented above. But it can also be understood in the sense that man in the State has the right to follow, according to his conscience, the will of God and to fulfill his commandments without any impediment. This freedom, true freedom, freedom worthy of the children of God, which so gloriously protects the dignity of the human person, is above all violence and all oppression and has always been the object of the desires and love of the Church. This is the freedom that the apostles constantly claimed for themselves, this is the freedom that the apologists confirmed with their writings, this is the freedom that the countless Christian martyrs consecrated with their blood. And rightly so, because the supreme authority of God over men and the supreme duty of man towards God find a definitive testimony in this Christian freedom. This Christian freedom has nothing in common with the spirit of sedition and disobedience. Nor does it intend to abrogate the respect due to public power, because human power as long as it has the right to command and demand obedience as long as it does not deviate from divine power and remains within the order established by God. But when human power commands something clearly contrary to divine will, it crosses the limits it has set and enters into conflict with divine authority. In this case it is fair not to obey.

22. On the contrary, the supporters of liberalism, who attribute to the State a despotic and unlimited power and affirm that we must live without taking God into account at all, totally reject this freedom of which we speak, and which is so closely linked to virtue and religion. And they describe as a crime against the State everything that is done to preserve this Christian freedom. If they were consistent with their principles, man would be obliged, according to them, to obey any government, no matter how tyrannical.

23. The Church ardently desires that these Christian teachings that we have summarily exposed be penetrated and practiced in all levels of society. All of these teachings have a marvelous effectiveness in remedying the neither small nor slight current evils, born in large part from those same freedoms that, proclaimed with so many dithyrambs, seemed to harbor within themselves the seeds of well-being and glory. These hopes have been disappointed by the facts. Instead of pleasant and healthy fruits we have gathered bitter and corrupt fruits. If the remedy is sought, look for it in the reestablishment of healthy principles, from which alone and exclusively the preservation of order and the guarantee, therefore, of true freedom can be confidently expected. Despite this, the Church takes maternal responsibility for the serious weight of human weaknesses. The Church does not ignore the trajectory that describes the spiritual and political history of our times. For this reason, even granting rights solely and exclusively to truth and virtue, the Church does not, however, oppose the tolerance by public powers of some situations contrary to truth and justice to avoid a greater evil or to acquire or preserve a greater good. God himself, in his providence, although infinitely good and all-powerful, nevertheless allows the existence of some evils in the world, partly so that greater good is not prevented and partly so that greater evil is not ensued. It is fair to imitate in the political government the one that governs the world. Furthermore: since human authority cannot prevent all evils, it must "permit and leave unpunished many things that are, however, justly punished by divine Providence."

24. For greater clarity, we will briefly recapitulate the presentation made and deduce the practical consequences. The essential core is the following: it is absolutely necessary that man remain entirely under the effective and constant dependence on God. Consequently, a human freedom that is not submissive to God and subject to his will is totally inconceivable. Denying God this supreme dominion or refusing to accept it is not freedom, but abuse of freedom and rebellion against God. This is precisely the disposition of spirit that originates and constitutes the fundamental evil of liberalism. However, there are various forms that this presents, because the will can be separated from the obedience due to God or from the obedience due to those who participate in divine authority, in many ways and to very different degrees.

25. The greatest perversion of freedom, which constitutes at the same time the worst species of liberalism, consists in completely rejecting the supreme authority of God and refusing all obedience to him, both in public life and in private and domestic life. Everything we have explained up to this point refers to this type of liberalism.

26. The second class is the system of those liberals who, on the one hand, recognize the need to submit to God, creator, lord of the world and provident governor of nature; but, on the other hand, they boldly reject the norms of dogma and morality that, surpassing nature, are communicated by God himself, or at least they claim that there is no reason to take them into account especially in the political life of the State. We previously exposed the dimensions of this error and the great inconsistency of these liberals. This doctrine is the main source of the pernicious theory of separation between Church and State; when, on the contrary, it is evident that both powers, although different in mission and unequal in dignity, must collaborate with each other and complete each other.

27. Two specifically different opinions fit within this generic error. Many seek the total and absolute separation between the Church and the State, in such a way that the entire legal system, institutions, customs, laws, State positions, the education of youth, remain outside the Church, as if it did not exist. They grant citizens, at most, the power, if they wish, to exercise religion in private. Against these liberals, the arguments with which we have rejected the theory of separation between Church and State remain in full force, with the aggravating factor that it is a complete absurdity that the Church is respected by the citizen and at the same time despised by the State.

28. Others admit the existence of the Church - denying it would be impossible - but they deny the nature and rights of a perfect society and affirm that the Church lacks legislative, judicial and coercive power, and that it only has the exhortative, persuasive and guiding function with respect to those who spontaneously and voluntarily submit to it. This theory falsifies the nature of this divine society, weakens and restricts its authority, its magisterium; in a word: all its effectiveness, at the same time so exaggerating the influence and power of the State, that the Church of God is subject to the jurisdiction and power of the State as if it were a mere civil association. The arguments used by the apologists, which We have particularly recalled in the encyclical Immortale Dei, are more than sufficient to demonstrate the error of this theory. Apologetics demonstrates that by the will of God the Church possesses all the characteristics and all the rights of a legitimate, supreme and totally perfect society.

29. Finally, there are many who do not approve of the separation between Church and State, but judge that the Church must adapt to the times, yielding and accommodating itself to the demands of modern prudence in the public administration of the State. This opinion is correct if it refers to a reasonable condescension that can be reconciled with truth and justice; That is to say, that the Church, with the proven hope of a very notable good, shows itself indulgent and grants to circumstances what it can grant them without violating the sanctity of its mission. But things change completely when it comes to practices and doctrines introduced against all rights due to the decadence of morality and the intellectual aberration of spirits. No historical period can live without religion, without truth, without justice. And since these supreme sacred realities have been entrusted by God himself to the protection of the Church, there is nothing so contrary to the Church as expecting her to surreptitiously tolerate error and injustice or favor with her connivance that which harms religion.

30. From the considerations presented, it follows that it is totally illegal to ask for, defend, or grant freedom of thought, of the press, of teaching, of worship, like so many other rights given by nature to man. For if man had really received these rights from nature, he would have the right to reject the authority of God and human freedom could not be limited by any law. It follows, furthermore, that these freedoms, if there are just causes, can be tolerated, but within certain limits so that they do not degenerate into an insolent disorder. Where these freedoms are in force, let citizens use them for good, but think about them the same as the Church thinks. A freedom should not be considered legitimate except when it represents an increase in the ease of living according to virtue. Outside of this case, never.

31. Where there already exists or where the existence is threatened by a government that has the nation unjustly oppressed by violation or forcibly deprives the Church of its due freedom, it is lawful to provide the State with another more moderate political organization, under which it can act freely. In this case, an immoderate and vicious freedom is not intended; relief is sought for the common good of all; This is only intended to ensure that where license for evil is granted, the right to do good is not impeded.

32. Nor is it prohibited in itself to prefer for the State a form of government moderated by the democratic element, always saving the Catholic doctrine regarding the origin and exercise of political power. The Church does not condemn any form of government, as long as the usefulness of the citizens is suitable in itself. But it requires, in accordance with nature, that each of these forms be established without harming anyone and, above all, fully respecting the rights of the Church.

33. It is good to participate in political life, unless in some places, due to circumstances of time and situation, another behavior is imposed. Even more: the Church approves the personal collaboration of everyone with their work for the common good and that each one, to the extent of his or her strength, seeks the defense, conservation and prosperity of the State.

34. Nor does the Church condemn the desire to free oneself from the domination of a foreign power or a tyrant, provided that this desire can be realized without violating justice. Nor does it rebuke, finally, those who seek to ensure that States live in accordance with their own legislation and that citizens enjoy broader means to increase their well-being. The Church has always been a faithful defender of moderate civic liberties. This is demonstrated above all by the cities of Italy, which achieved, under municipal rule, prosperity, wealth and glorious name in those times when the healthy influence of the Church had penetrated without opposition from anyone into all parts of the State.

35. These teachings, venerable brothers, which, dictated by faith and reason at the same time, we have transmitted to you in fulfillment of our apostolic office, we trust will be fruitful for many, mainly by uniting your efforts with ours. We, with humility of heart, raise our supplicating eyes to God and with all fervor ask him to deign to graciously grant to men the light of his wisdom and his counsel, so that, strengthened by his virtue, they may see the truth in such important things and live according to the truth, both in private and public life, at all times and with unwavering constancy.
